title: Bed Assist Handles: What to Check Before You Buy One
subtitle: A bed assist handle can make getting out of bed easier, but it comes with fit and safety questions worth settling first.
excerpt: A bed assist handle gives you something solid to hold when you sit up and stand. Here is how to check that one fits your bed, avoids dangerous gaps, and suits the person using it.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Getting out of bed is something many of us never think about until it gets harder. A bed assist handle is one gadget people consider to make sitting up and standing a little easier.

A bed assist handle is a simple steel frame that gives you something sturdy to hold as you sit up and stand. It can help. It also comes with a real safety concern that every buyer should understand first.
How a bed assist handle works

A handle stands up at the side of the bed for you to grip as you rise. The models in our notes include a safety strap that secures to the bed frame. Each maker has its own bed and mattress limits, so read those before you buy.

Be clear about what it does not do. A handle gives leverage for sitting up and standing, nothing more. It will not stop someone from rolling out of bed, it is not an alarm or fall detector, and it does not replace supervision for a person who needs help.

The main hazard is entrapment, which means a person gets caught in a gap between the mattress and the rail. Consumer Reports reports that the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) counted about 300 adult deaths from January 2003 to September 2021. Of those, 92 percent involved entrapment, and most of the victims were 70 or older. A mandatory standard for adult portable bed rails took effect in August 2023.

Consumer Reports tested 10 adult portable rails, and four failed breakage or entrapment tests. It also says the words "ASTM Approved" on a listing mean little. Nancy Cowles, formerly of Kids In Danger, told the magazine: "That's not a meaningful claim. ASTM doesn't approve or certify anything." The FDA suggests checking for compliance with the standard by name, ASTM F3186-17. Consumer Reports suggests looking for CPSC compliance and third-party lab testing.

The FDA lists people at higher risk, including those with confusion, dementia, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, balance disorders, a past stroke or low blood pressure. If that describes the person you are shopping for, talk with their doctor first. For someone with confusion or dementia, a handle should only be used with a clinician's advice. A low bed and floor mats may suit them better. The FDA also lists lowering the bed, roll guards, foam bumpers, concave mattresses and a bed trapeze as alternatives to rails, and says rails are not a substitute for monitoring.

items: Start with your bed type. Some handles do not fit adjustable bases, and one model below fits only metal hospital beds with 6-inch mattresses.

Check mattress thickness and softness against the maker's limits. For example, the Stander Wonder lists 6 to 14 inch mattresses, and its FAQ says it is not for extra-soft ones. The FDA notes that soft mattresses, toppers and air mattresses can create gaps.
Look for the standard named plainly, ASTM F3186-17, rather than "ASTM approved" wording alone. Check the model's CPSC recall status before buying.
Check the weight capacity against the user's weight. Both home models below list 300 lb.
Watch for hidden steps: one seller requires a prescription or professional license check, shipping may add cost, and most handles need assembly. No page we read showed a subscription.
Compare prices, warranty and return terms. Prices can differ by seller for the same model.
Buy new. Consumer Reports warns against used rails.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Follow the maker's guide step by step and secure the safety strap to the bed frame as directed. Then look closely for any gap between the mattress and the handle. If you see one, fix it before anyone sleeps in the bed.
"always double-check to make sure the bed rail can't be moved away from the mattress" — Courtney Griffin, Consumer Federation of America, in Consumer Reports

Mattresses shift, so inspect the fit regularly and recheck it after changing sheets or moving the bed. Choose and place the handle so it does not invite climbing over it. If the person might climb over a rail to get out of bed, a handle is not the right tool.

A bed handle is not the only option. Consumer Reports suggests wall-mounted grab bars or transfer poles as alternatives, and the FDA lists lowering the bed among its alternatives to rails. Ask the person's doctor which approach suits them.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A good bed handle is a modest, sturdy helper. Check your bed type, look for gaps, and ask the doctor if there are health concerns, especially confusion or dementia. Those habits help keep a useful tool a safe one.

products.name: Stander Wonder Bed Handle
products.blurb: For traditional, non-adjustable beds with 6 to 14 inch mattresses; it has a padded handle, a safety strap that secures to the bed frame and a 300 lb capacity, and the page states it passed ASTM F3186-17. Not for adjustable beds or extra-soft mattresses. Stock is unclear: Stander's collection page shows it as "Sold out" while the product page reads as available, so confirm before ordering.

products.name: Drive Medical M-Rail Home Bed Assist Handle (1222P)
products.blurb: An M-shaped steel handle with several grab points and an extra-long safety strap; the reseller's page says it works for single, twin, double, queen and king beds, with a 300 lb capacity and limited-lifetime warranty. Details come from Vitality Medical, an authorized reseller, not Drive's own site. Vitality requires a prescription or professional license and verifies it before shipping, so allow extra time.

products.name: Stander EZ Click LTC Bed Handle, set of 2
products.price: $349.99 for the set of two (price on page, November 2026)
products.blurb: Made only for metal hospital or institutional beds with 6-inch mattresses, with a 500 lb capacity. A good example of why bed type comes first: it is not meant for most home beds.
